# Overview

This vignette goes through the methods of `rcausality()` one by one. For
every method it gives the **full reference** of the paper it implements,
explains the **idea** and what exactly is implemented, names **where in
the paper** the reproduced result is, and runs a **reduced reproduction**
with figures. The full-size reproduction scripts are installed with the
package (`system.file("reproduce", package = "Rcausality")`) and their
results are summarised in the README; the sizes here are kept small so
that the vignette builds in a couple of minutes, so numbers are noisier
than in the scripts. The last section compares the methods on common
benchmarks.

| `method` | Reference | Kind of system |
|---|---|---|
| `"granger"`, `"bayes_granger"` | Granger (1969); Geweke (1982); Kass & Raftery (1995); Liang et al. (2008) | linear, stochastic |
| `"cmi"`, `"cmi_lag"` | Frenzel & Pompe (2007); Runge (2018); Zlatniczki et al. (2021) | non-linear, stochastic; hidden common driver |
| `"markov"` | Stippinger et al. (2023) | stochastic dynamical systems |
| `"df"` | Telcs, Kurbucz & Jakovac (2025) | deterministic or stochastic |
| `"dc"` | Benko et al. (2024) | deterministic (chaotic) |
| `"ccdh"` | Stippinger et al. (2023) | deterministic; hidden common cause |
| `"dfe"` | Jakovac et al. (manuscript) | binary / stochastic |
| `"pid"` | Telcs (2026); Mages et al. (2024) | stochastic, information atoms |
| `"hirata"` | Hirata & Aihara (2010) | deterministic; hidden common cause |
| `"cd"` | Krakovska (2019) | deterministic |
| `"te"`, `"ccm"` | Schreiber (2000); Sugihara et al. (2012) | baselines |
| `"pcmci"` (optional) | Runge et al. (2019) | many autocorrelated variables |

# Granger causality and its Bayesian variants

<div class="paper">
Granger, C. W. J. (1969). Investigating causal relations by econometric
models and cross-spectral methods. *Econometrica*, 37(3), 424-438.
<https://doi.org/10.2307/1912791><br>
Geweke, J. (1982). Measurement of linear dependence and feedback between
multiple time series. *JASA*, 77(378), 304-313.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1982.10477803><br>
Kass, R. E. and Raftery, A. E. (1995). Bayes factors. *JASA*, 90(430),
773-795. <https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1995.10476572><br>
Liang, F., Paulo, R., Molina, G., Clyde, M. A. and Berger, J. O. (2008).
Mixtures of g priors for Bayesian variable selection. *JASA*, 103(481),
410-423. <https://doi.org/10.1198/016214507000001337>
</div>

**Idea.** $x$ Granger-causes $y$ if the lags of $x$ improve the linear
prediction of $y_t$ beyond the lags of $y$ (and of the control series in
the conditional version). The restricted model $y_t = a_0 + \sum_l a_l
y_{t-l} + \varepsilon_t$ is compared with the unrestricted one that adds
$\sum_l b_l x_{t-l}$ by an F-test; Geweke's measure $\log(RSS_r/RSS_u)$
is the effect size.

**Bayesian decision.** `bayes = TRUE` turns the regression into a
Bayesian one (`bayes_control()`): stochastic-search variable selection
over the cause's lags (`prior = "spike_slab"`, George and McCulloch 1993;
posterior inclusion probability per lag, exact enumeration of the lag
subsets), a block comparison with a normal slab (`"normal"`), or the
closed-form factors: the Schwarz (BIC) approximation
$\log BF_{10} \approx (BIC_r - BIC_u)/2$, the exact factor under Zellner's
g-prior with $g = n$ (`"g"`) and under the hyper-g prior of Liang et al.
(2008) (`"hyper_g"`). Posterior draws give credible intervals of Geweke's
measure. Evidence labels follow Kass and Raftery. Every other method has a
Bayesian variant as well (a Bayesian surrogate test with an effect-size
prior, a prior over the causal cases, a Bayesian Markov decision table);
see `vignette("rcausality")`.

```{r granger}
d <- sim_var(400, "x_to_y", seed = 1)
bf <- sapply(c("spike_slab", "normal", "bic", "g", "hyper_g"), function(pr)
  rcausality(d, bayes = TRUE, control = bayes_control(prior = pr, n_iter = 200, chains = 1))$pairs$bf10)
rownames(bf) <- c("y -> x", "x -> y"); signif(bf, 3)
```

The five factors agree: overwhelming evidence for `x -> y`, evidence
against `y -> x` (the hyper-g factor is the least extreme, as expected
from its heavier-tailed prior).

```{r granger-lags, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "The lag scan of the Granger statistic on the VAR(1) pair: the evidence for x -> y is strongest at lag 1 and decays, y -> x stays at the noise level."}
plot(rcausality(d), "lags")
```

# Zlatniczki et al. (2021): lag-shifted conditional mutual information

<div class="paper">
Zlatniczki, A., Stippinger, M., Benko, Z., Somogyvari, Z. and Telcs, A.
(2021). Relaxation of some confusions about confounders. *Entropy*,
23(11), 1450. <https://doi.org/10.3390/e23111450><br>
Frenzel, S. and Pompe, B. (2007). Partial mutual information for
coupling analysis of multivariate time series. *Physical Review
Letters*, 99, 204101. <https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.204101><br>
Runge, J. (2018). Conditional independence testing based on a
nearest-neighbor estimator of conditional mutual information. *AISTATS
2018*, PMLR 84, 938-947.
</div>

**Idea.** *Relation 1* (Sect. 2.1) decides between $A \to B$, $B \to A$,
no coupling and a common driver from three conditional mutual
informations: the lagged ones $I_A = I(A_{t-\tau}; B_t \mid B\text{-past},
A\text{-past})$ and $I_B$ (the reverse), and the contemporaneous one
$I^{(k)} = I(A_t; B_t \mid \text{both pasts})$. A directed link shows up
in one lagged quantity and leaves $I^{(k)} = 0$, whereas a common driver
leaves both lagged quantities at zero but makes $I^{(k)} > 0$. Sect. 2.7
and Appendix A discuss the convergence of these quantities in the history
depth; Sects. 2.4-2.6 relate the delays of the three processes by a
triangle inequality (`lag_triangle_check()`).

**Implemented.** `method = "cmi_lag"`: the CMIs are estimated with the
Frenzel-Pompe kNN estimator (`knn_cmi()`), tested with Runge's
local-permutation scheme (`local_permutation_test()`); the
contemporaneous test adds the `common_cause` class. The paper is
theoretical (no numerical experiments), so the reproduction illustrates
its propositions on systems with known truth.

```{r zlatniczki}
set.seed(5); n <- 400
e1 <- rnorm(n); e2 <- 0.8 * e1 + 0.6 * rnorm(n)        # shared innovation = hidden common driver
common <- data.frame(x = as.numeric(stats::filter(e1, 0.5, "recursive")),
                     y = as.numeric(stats::filter(e2, 0.5, "recursive")))
r_dir <- rcausality(sim_var(n, "x_to_y", seed = 1), method = "cmi_lag", lag = 1, seed = 1)
r_com <- rcausality(common, method = "cmi_lag", lag = 1, seed = 1)
rbind(direct = c(class = r_dir$classes$class, instant_p = signif(r_dir$instant$p_value, 2)),
      common = c(class = r_com$classes$class, instant_p = signif(r_com$instant$p_value, 2)))
```

Appendix A: the contemporaneous CMI of the common-driver pair stays
positive as the conditioning history grows, that of the directly driven
pair stays at zero.

```{r zlatniczki-conv, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Convergence of the contemporaneous CMI in the history depth (Zlatniczki et al. 2021, Appendix A)."}
dd <- sim_var(n, "x_to_y", seed = 1)
cv <- cbind(common_driver = cmi_convergence(common$x, common$y, lag = 0, depths = 1:4)$cmi,
            direct_link   = cmi_convergence(dd$x, dd$y, lag = 0, depths = 1:4)$cmi)
matplot(1:4, cv, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, lty = 1, col = c("#B2403A", "#2B5C8A"), xlab = "history depth d",
        ylab = "I(x[t]; y[t] | pasts of depth d)", xaxt = "n", main = "Contemporaneous CMI vs history depth", font.main = 2)
axis(1, 1:4); abline(h = 0, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
legend("topright", c("common driver", "direct link x -> y"), col = c("#B2403A", "#2B5C8A"), lwd = 2, pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

# Stippinger et al. (2023): the Markov-chain approach

<div class="paper">
Stippinger, M., Bencze, A., Zlatniczki, A., Somogyvari, Z. and Telcs, A.
(2023). Causal discovery of stochastic dynamical systems: a Markov chain
approach. *Mathematics*, 11(4), 852.
<https://doi.org/10.3390/math11040852>
</div>

**Idea.** An autonomous process is Markov in its own state; a *driven*
process is not, because the driver acts as hidden memory; the lagged
joint state $(x_t, y_{t+1})$ of a driver and its driven process is Markov
again, while the joint of two processes with a hidden common cause is
not. Testing the Markov property of $x$, $y$ and the joint therefore
gives a causal verdict (decision tables (10)-(12), Sect. 4).

**Implemented.** `markov_test()` for discrete states uses exact
contingency tables conditional on the present state; for continuous
states it follows Algorithms 1-2 of the paper (kNN conditions of size
$\sqrt{n}$, local random projections, two bins, Yates-corrected modified
log-likelihood test, local-permutation surrogates of the futures). The
local p-values are aggregated by a clipped geometric mean (the paper uses
the harmonic mean, `aggregate = "harmonic"`).

**Reproduced.** Sect. 6.1, the "turn-wheel" example of Figure 2: Alice is
a two-state Markov chain that drives Bob and Barry with one step delay.

```{r markov}
w <- sim_turnwheel(2000, seed = 1); N <- nrow(w)
mp <- function(x) markov_test(x, m = 1, n_perm = 49, seed = 1)$p_value
pv <- c(alice = mp(w$alice), bob = mp(w$bob), barry = mp(w$barry),
        `alice[t] x bob[t+1]` = mp(cbind(w$alice[-N], w$bob[-1])), `bob x barry` = mp(cbind(w$bob, w$barry)))
round(pv, 3)
```

```{r markov-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Markov-property p-values of the turn-wheel series (Stippinger et al. 2023, Fig. 2): the driver and the lagged driver-driven joint are Markov, the driven series and the joint of the two driven series are not."}
bp <- barplot(pv, col = ifelse(pv < 0.05, "#B2403A", "#1B7A43"), ylim = c(0, 1), ylab = "p-value of the Markov test",
              names.arg = rep("", 5), border = "grey40", main = "Turn-wheel: who is Markov?", font.main = 2)
mtext(names(pv), side = 1, at = bp, line = 1, cex = 0.75); abline(h = 0.05, lty = 3, col = "grey40")
legend("topleft", c("Markov (p >= 0.05)", "not Markov"), fill = c("#1B7A43", "#B2403A"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The decision table in `rcausality()`:

```{r markov-rc}
rcausality(w[1:800, c("alice", "bob")], method = "markov", memory = 1, n_perm = 49, n_markov = 49, seed = 1)$classes$relation
```

# Telcs, Kurbucz and Jakovac (2025): degrees of freedom

<div class="paper">
Telcs, A., Kurbucz, M. T. and Jakovac, A. (2025). Unified causality
analysis based on the degrees of freedom. *Physical Review E*, 112(1),
014204. <https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.112.014204>
</div>

**Idea.** The *order* (number of degrees of freedom) of a process is the
number of past values that have to be fixed for the present value to be
determined: constrain the past within windows of width $\sigma_W$ and
watch the conditional spread $\sigma$ of the present (Definition 1,
Sect. 6.1). With $N$ constraints the $\sigma(\sigma_W)$ curve is flat
(saturated) while $N$ is below the order and proportional to the width
once the past is fully constrained. Table 2 reads the orders of $x$, $y$
and the joint process as a causal case ($d_{xy} = d_y > d_x$ means
$x \to y$; $d_{xy} = d_x + d_y$ independence; $\max < d_{xy} < d_x +
d_y$ a hidden common cause). Sect. 7 adds the directed test "constrain
the cause's past and watch the effect's spread".

**Implemented.** `df_variance()` with adaptive (kNN) windows and a
local-permutation test of every added constraint, plus the
$\sigma(\sigma_W, N)$ profile of the paper; `rcausality(method = "df")`
estimates the three orders and applies Table 2 whenever it is
determinate, otherwise the directed tests.

**Reproduced.** The linear rotation system of Sect. 6.4 (Eqs. 25-30,
Figs. 1-2): a two-dimensional rotation $z$ drives $x$ and $y$.

```{r df, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "sigma(sigma_W, N) profile of the z subsystem (Telcs et al. 2025, Figs. 1-2): the N = 0 line is flat, every N >= 1 line is proportional to the width, so one constraint determines z."}
d <- sim_df_rotation(800, "deterministic", seed = 1)
dz <- df_variance(d[, c("z1", "z2")], max_constr = 3, n_perm = 29, seed = 1)
dz
plot(dz)
```

The Table-2 reading on the pair $(z_1, x_1)$: $x$ has order 4 (its own
two lags plus the two of $z$ that it carries), $z$ order 2, the joint
order 4, hence $z \to x$. The directed tests alone would read the
deterministic pair as bidirectional, because the driven series
reconstructs its driver.

```{r df2}
d <- sim_df_rotation(1500, "deterministic", seed = 1)
r <- rcausality(d[, c("z1", "x1")], method = "df", lag = 1, max_constr = 4, n_perm = 39, seed = 1)
r$df[, c("df_x", "df_y", "df_joint", "table2", "decided_by")]
r$classes$relation
```

# Benko et al. (2024): Bayesian dimensional causality

<div class="paper">
Benko, Z., Zlatniczki, A., Stippinger, M., Fabo, D., Solyom, A., Eross,
L., Telcs, A. and Somogyvari, Z. (2024). Bayesian inference of causal
relations between dynamical systems. *Chaos, Solitons & Fractals*, 185,
115142. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chaos.2024.115142><br>
Farahmand, A. M., Szepesvari, C. and Audibert, J.-Y. (2007).
Manifold-adaptive dimension estimation. *ICML 2007*, 265-272.
<https://doi.org/10.1145/1273496.1273530>
</div>

**Idea.** By Takens' theorem the delay embedding of a driven system
contains the driver, so the intrinsic dimensions of the embedded $X$,
$Y$, their joint $J$ and an "independent joint" $Z$ (the joint of $X$
with a shuffled $Y$) obey different relations in the five causal cases
(Eqs. 1-4): $D_X = D_J < D_Y$ ... for $X \to Y$ (the joint is no larger
than the driven system), $D_J = D_X + D_Y = D_Z$ for independence,
$\max(D_X, D_Y) < D_J < D_Z$ for a hidden common cause. Dimensions are
estimated with the Farahmand kNN estimator at several $k$, and Appendix
A.2 integrates the dimension likelihoods over nine events to a
posterior probability of the cases.

**Implemented.** `dimensional_causality()` (written from the paper; the
authors' AGPL reference code was not used), rank normalisation,
$J = $ embedding of $a x + y$ with $a = \sqrt{29/31}$, effective sample
size $n/(2k)$, grid integration of the likelihoods.

**Reproduced.** Appendix B.2 and Figure 1: three coupled logistic maps
(`sim_logistic_bdc()`, $r = 3.99$, $\beta = 0.5$), all five patterns.

```{r dc, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Dimensional causality on the hidden-common-cause pattern (Benko et al. 2024, Fig. 1): D_X = D_Y < D_J < D_Z and the posterior concentrates on the common cause."}
db <- sim_logistic_bdc(2000, "common_cause", seed = 1)
dc <- dimensional_causality(db$x, db$y, m = 4, k_range = seq(12, 36, by = 8), seed = 1)
dc
plot(dc)
```

```{r dc-all}
sapply(c("x_to_y", "bidirectional", "common_cause", "independent"), function(sc) {
  dd <- sim_logistic_bdc(1500, sc, seed = 2)
  dimensional_causality(dd$x, dd$y, m = 4, k_range = seq(12, 36, by = 8), seed = 1)$best
})
```

# Stippinger et al. (2023): CCDH, complexity-based discovery of a hidden common cause

<div class="paper">
Stippinger, M., Varga, B., Benko, Z., Fabo, D., Eross, L., Telcs, A. and
Somogyvari, Z. (2023). CCDH: Complexity based causal discovery of hidden
common cause in time series. *Chaos, Solitons & Fractals*, 176, 114054.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chaos.2023.114054><br>
Nagaraj, N., Balasubramanian, K. and Dey, S. (2013). A new complexity
measure for time series analysis and classification. *Eur. Phys. J.
Special Topics*, 222, 847-860. <https://doi.org/10.1140/epjst/e2013-01888-9>
</div>

**Idea.** The rank-order patterns of an embedded series are compressed
with NSRPS (non-sequential recursive pair substitution, Sect. 2); the
compression-rate curve $cr_k$ measures complexity. If $y$ drives $x$, the
lagged $y$ is a function of the embedding of $x$, so the *skewed joint*
$(x_t, \dots, x_{t-m+2}, y_{t-m+1})$ is as compressible as $x$ alone;
if $x$ drives $y$ the same holds for the other joint; both hold for
mutual coupling; neither for a hidden common cause (Propositions 1-3,
Sect. 3).

**Implemented.** `ccdh()` with the NSRPS compressor in C++, circular-shift
surrogates (the paper leaves the significance test open) and the
reconstruction index $\Delta / \Delta_{\text{surrogate}}$ thresholded at
`theta = 0.45`. The worked NSRPS example of Appendix 7.1 is reproduced
exactly in the tests.

**Reproduced.** Sect. 4, Figure 1: coupled logistic maps with a driver
(`sim_logistic3()`).

```{r ccdh, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "CCDH compression curves (Stippinger et al., Fig. 1a): the joint of the driven x1 with the driver x0 is as compressible as x1 alone, the other joint is not."}
d3 <- sim_logistic3(1000, "driver", b = 0.4, seed = 3)        # x0 drives x1 and x2
cc <- ccdh(d3$x0, d3$x1, m = 3, n_surr = 30, seed = 1)
cc
plot(cc)
```

```{r ccdh2}
ccdh(d3$x1, d3$x2, m = 3, n_surr = 30, seed = 1)$verdict        # both driven by the hidden x0
dm <- sim_logistic3(1000, "mutual", c = 0.4, seed = 3)
ccdh(dm$x1, dm$x2, m = 3, n_surr = 30, seed = 1)$verdict        # mutual coupling
```

# Jakovac et al.: the degrees-of-freedom method with conditional entropies

<div class="paper">
Jakovac, A., Fabo, D., Eross, L., Stippinger, M., Benko, Z., Somogyvari,
Z. and Telcs, A. Causality beyond the Reichenbach principle: the
degrees-of-freedom method (manuscript). Builds on Telcs, Kurbucz and
Jakovac (2025), *Physical Review E*, 112(1), 014204.
</div>

**Idea.** The df relations of Table 1 are read from conditional
entropies instead of conditional variances: the series are binarised,
the surfaces $H(x_t \mid x\text{-past of length } L, y\text{-past of
length } K)$ are computed with surrogate-corrected versions, and
curvature and asymmetry features of the surfaces are classified by a
random forest trained on coupled binary Markov chains (Sect. 2, Appendix
F; Figs. 2-3 report 92 % accuracy at length 2000).

**Implemented.** `dfe_classify()` with the feature set of Appendix F plus
the surrogate-corrected surfaces, `dfe_train()` (a 200-per-class model is
trained at first use), `sim_markov_pair()`. Needs the `ranger` package;
a small model is trained here.

```{r dfe, eval = has_ranger, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Conditional-entropy surfaces of a coupled binary pair and the class probabilities of the random forest (Jakovac et al.)."}
m <- dfe_train(n_per_class = 30, lengths = c(500, 1000), seed = 1)
dp <- sim_markov_pair(1500, "x_to_y", seed = 3)
fe <- dfe_classify(dp$x, dp$y, model = m)
fe
plot(fe)
```

# Telcs (2026): finite-resolution MAR-PID

<div class="paper">
Telcs, A. (2026). Empirical nonnegative finite-resolution MAR-PID for
continuous variables. *Entropy*, 28(6), 641.
<https://doi.org/10.3390/e28060641><br>
Mages, T., Anastasiadi, E. and Rohner, C. (2024). Non-negative
decomposition of multivariate information: from minimum to blackwell
specific information. *Entropy*, 26(5), 424.
<https://doi.org/10.3390/e26050424>
</div>

**Idea.** The mutual information of two sources about a target is
decomposed into *redundant*, *unique* and *synergistic* atoms. Continuous
variables are binarised recursively by quantiles (Sect. 3), the atoms
are computed bit by bit from the zonogons of the source channels in the
Blackwell order (Sects. 4-5) and aggregated over the target bits. In
`rcausality(method = "pid")` the sources are the cause's past and the
effect's own past, the target the effect's future, and the directed
statistic is the unique + synergistic ("novel") information of the
cause's past, tested with surrogates.

**Reproduced.** Sect. 6.2, Table 2: a mixed redundancy-synergy example
in which $A = V_1 \oplus V_2$ with probability $q$ and $A = V_1 = V_2$
otherwise ($q = 0$: pure redundancy, $q = 1$: pure synergy).

```{r pid, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "MAR-PID atoms of the mixed example (Telcs 2026, Table 2): redundancy at q = 0 turns into synergy at q = 1."}
set.seed(1); n <- 2000; qs <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
atoms <- sapply(qs, function(q) {
  V1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5); V2 <- ifelse(runif(n) < q, rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), V1)
  A <- ifelse(runif(n) < q, as.integer(xor(V1, V2)), V1)
  marpid(A, V1, V2, k_target = 1, k_source = 1)$atoms[c("redundant", "unique_1", "unique_2", "synergy")]
})
colnames(atoms) <- paste0("q = ", qs); round(atoms, 2)
barplot(atoms, col = c("#1B7A43", "#2B5C8A", "#7FB3D5", "#B2403A"), border = "grey40", ylab = "bits",
        main = "Information atoms of A about (V1, V2)", font.main = 2, legend.text = rownames(atoms),
        args.legend = list(x = "top", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.8, inset = -0.02), ylim = c(0, 1.25))
```

```{r pid-rc}
rcausality(sim_var(600, "x_to_y", seed = 1), method = "pid", lag = 1, seed = 1)$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "statistic", "p_adj", "significant")]
```

# Hirata and Aihara (2010): recurrence plots

<div class="paper">
Hirata, Y. and Aihara, K. (2010). Identifying hidden common causes from
bivariate time series by using the recurrence plot. *Physical Review E*,
81, 016203. <https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.81.016203><br>
Marwan, N., Romano, M. C., Thiel, M. and Kurths, J. (2007). Recurrence
plots for the analysis of complex systems. *Physics Reports*, 438(5-6),
237-329. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2006.11.001>
</div>

**Idea.** A recurrence plot marks the pairs of times $(i, j)$ at which
the embedded state returns to itself. Two criteria: (1) related series
recur *simultaneously* far more often than independent ones (joint
recurrence rate over the product of the rates); (2) if $x$ drives $y$,
the state of $y$ determines that of $x$, so every recurrence of $y$ is
also a recurrence of $x$: the *coverage* $P(R_X \mid R_Y)$ is close to
one, and non-coverage denies the direction. Simultaneous recurrences
without coverage in either direction indicate a hidden common cause.

**Implemented.** `hirata_rp()` with tight (rate/5) recurrences
conditioned on and loose (rate) ones covering, circular-shift surrogates,
a coverage index threshold. The full text was not available to us; the
implementation follows the abstract and the standard recurrence-plot
definitions.

```{r hirata, dev = "png", dpi = 110, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Recurrence plots of a driver x, a driven y, and the coverage picture: the tight recurrences of y that fall on recurrences of x (green) versus those that do not (red)."}
dh <- sim_logistic_bdc(800, "x_to_y", seed = 1)
h <- hirata_rp(dh$x, dh$y, E = 3, n_surr = 50, seed = 1)
h
plot(h)
```

# Krakovska (2019): correlation-dimension relations

<div class="paper">
Krakovska, A. (2019). Correlation dimension detects causal links in
coupled dynamical systems. *Entropy*, 21(9), 818.
<https://doi.org/10.3390/e21090818><br>
Krakovska, A., Jakubik, J., Chvostekova, M., Coufal, D., Jajcay, N. and
Palus, M. (2018). Comparison of six methods for the detection of
causality in a bivariate time series. *Physical Review E*, 97, 042207.
<https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.97.042207>
</div>

**Idea.** The Grassberger-Procaccia correlation dimensions of $X$, $Y$,
their joint and an independent joint obey the same relations as the
intrinsic dimensions of the dimensional method; the relations are tested
with bootstrap standard errors (plus a 10 % relative tolerance here).

```{r krakovska, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Correlation sums of X, Y and the joint of the driven pair: the slopes (dimensions) of X and the joint coincide when x drives y."}
kc <- krakovska_cd(dh$x, dh$y, E = 3, n_boot = 10, seed = 1)
kc
ex <- embed_delay(dh$x, 3); ey <- embed_delay(dh$y, 3); ej <- embed_delay(sqrt(29 / 31) * dh$x + dh$y, 3)
cs <- lapply(list(X = ex, Y = ey, joint = ej), corr_dim, n_boot = 0)
plot(NA, xlim = range(sapply(cs, function(z) range(log(z$radii)))), ylim = range(sapply(cs, function(z) range(log(z$corr_sum)))),
     xlab = "log r", ylab = "log C(r)", main = "Correlation sums (Grassberger-Procaccia)", font.main = 2)
cols <- c("#B2403A", "#2B5C8A", "#1B7A43")
for (i in 1:3) { z <- cs[[i]]; lines(log(z$radii), log(z$corr_sum), col = cols[i], lwd = 2); points(log(z$radii), log(z$corr_sum), col = cols[i], pch = 16) }
legend("topleft", sprintf("%s: D2 = %.2f", names(cs), sapply(cs, `[[`, "d2")), col = cols, lwd = 2, pch = 16, bty = "n")
```

# Baselines: transfer entropy and convergent cross mapping

<div class="paper">
Schreiber, T. (2000). Measuring information transfer. *Physical Review
Letters*, 85(2), 461-464. <https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.461><br>
Marschinski, R. and Kantz, H. (2002). Analysing the information flow
between financial time series: an improved estimator for transfer
entropy. *European Physical Journal B*, 30, 275-281.
<https://doi.org/10.1140/epjb/e2002-00379-2><br>
Sugihara, G., May, R., Ye, H., Hsieh, C., Deyle, E., Fogarty, M. and
Munch, S. (2012). Detecting causality in complex ecosystems. *Science*,
338(6106), 496-500. <https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1227079>
</div>

**Transfer entropy** $T_{x \to y} = I(y_t; x_{t-k} \mid y_{t-l})$ on
binned series, with shuffle surrogates and the effective TE of
Marschinski and Kantz (observed minus mean surrogate). **Convergent cross
mapping** predicts $x$ from the delay embedding of $y$ by simplex
projection; if $x$ drives $y$, the skill $\rho$ of "$y$ cross-maps $x$"
rises and converges with the library size (Kendall test), and it is
compared with time-shift surrogates.

```{r baselines, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Convergent cross mapping on coupled logistic maps: the skill of y xmap x (x drives y) converges to a high value; the reverse stays low."}
lg <- sim_logistic(500, "x_to_y", seed = 2)
te <- transfer_entropy(lg$x, lg$y, n_surr = 100, seed = 1); c(TE = te$te, TE_eff = te$te_eff, p = te$p_value)
r1 <- ccm(lg$x, lg$y, E = 3, n_surr = 50, seed = 1); r2 <- ccm(lg$y, lg$x, E = 3, n_surr = 50, seed = 1)
plot(r1$rho$lib_size, r1$rho$rho, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "#2B5C8A", log = "x", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "library size", ylab = "cross-map skill rho", main = "CCM: convergence with the library size", font.main = 2)
lines(r2$rho$lib_size, r2$rho$rho, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = "#B2403A")
legend("right", c(sprintf("y xmap x (x -> y): rho = %.2f", r1$rho_max), sprintf("x xmap y (y -> x): rho = %.2f", r2$rho_max)),
       col = c("#2B5C8A", "#B2403A"), lwd = 2, pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

# Runge et al. (2019): PCMCI through tigramite (optional)

<div class="paper">
Runge, J., Nowack, P., Kretschmer, M., Flaxman, S. and Sejdinovic, D.
(2019). Detecting and quantifying causal associations in large nonlinear
time series datasets. *Science Advances*, 5(11), eaau4996.
<https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aau4996><br>
Runge, J. (2020). Discovering contemporaneous and lagged causal relations
in autocorrelated nonlinear time series datasets. *UAI 2020*, PMLR 124,
1388-1397.
</div>

**Idea.** PCMCI first selects the parents of every variable with the
PC$_1$ algorithm, then tests every lagged link with the momentary
conditional independence (MCI) test conditioned on the parents of both
variables, which controls false positives under autocorrelation;
PCMCI+ also orients contemporaneous links.

**Implemented.** `pcmci()` wraps the authors' Python package tigramite
through reticulate (nothing is ported) and maps the MCI statistics,
adjusted p-values and contemporaneous links onto a `causres`. The chunk
below runs only when tigramite is installed; the full reproduction
(`inst/reproduce/runge2019_pcmci.R`) recovers the four links of the
tigramite tutorial model exactly.

```{r pcmci, eval = has_tigramite}
net <- sim_var(500, n_series = 3, seed = 1)
rp <- pcmci(net, tau_max = 2)
rp$pairs[, c("cause", "effect", "lag", "statistic", "p_adj", "significant")]
```

# Comparing the methods

## Linear versus non-linear coupling

`compare_methods()` runs several methods on one data set. On a linear
VAR link the stochastic methods agree. On the chaotic logistic maps of
Benko et al. the picture splits: the regression- and binning-based tests
(`granger`, `te`) and CCM read the strong unidirectional coupling as
bidirectional (the driven system's past does carry information about
the driver, and the driver's embedding some about the driven system),
while the kNN-CMI test and the dimension-, recurrence- and
correlation-dimension methods return the true direction; CCDH reads
this particular realisation as a hidden common cause.

```{r compare1, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Verdicts on a linear VAR(1) link."}
cv <- compare_methods(sim_var(500, "x_to_y", seed = 1), methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "pid"), seed = 1, lag = 1)
cv$table
plot(cv)
```

```{r compare2, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Verdicts on the coupled logistic maps of Benko et al. (x drives y)."}
cl <- compare_methods(sim_logistic_bdc(500, "x_to_y", seed = 2), methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "ccm", "dc", "hirata", "cd", "ccdh"),
                      seed = 1, lag = 1)
cl$table
plot(cl)
```

## Benchmark on the five patterns of coupled logistic maps

`benchmark_methods()` scores the methods on simulated scenarios with
known truth. The five patterns of Benko et al. (2024) --
`sim_logistic_bdc()` -- are the natural benchmark for the
dynamical-systems methods; the stochastic ones are included for
contrast. Two replications per scenario keep the vignette fast; use many
more in practice.

```{r bench, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "Accuracy of the methods on the five coupled-logistic-map patterns (2 replications each, n = 500)."}
bm <- benchmark_methods(methods = c("granger", "te", "ccm", "dc", "ccdh", "hirata", "cd"),
                        scenarios = c("x_to_y", "bidirectional", "common_cause", "independent"),
                        simulator = sim_logistic_bdc, n = 500, reps = 2, seed = 1, args = list(te = list(lag = 1)))
bm
plot(bm)
```

At this length the recurrence and correlation-dimension criteria are the
most reliable; the dimensional method needs longer series (Benko et al.
use $N = 10^4$; the README reproduction at that length recovers all
four patterns), and the stochastic tests cannot tell a hidden common
cause from a directed link on deterministic data. The confusion matrices
show *how* a method fails, which matters more than the accuracy figure:
e.g. whether a hidden common cause is read as a directed link (a false
causal claim) or as independence (a missed relation).

```{r bench-conf}
bm$confusion$dc
bm$confusion$granger
```

## The same on stochastic data

```{r bench2, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Accuracy on linear VAR pairs."}
bv <- benchmark_methods(methods = c("granger", "cmi", "te", "pid"),
                        scenarios = c("x_to_y", "bidirectional", "independent"), simulator = sim_var,
                        n = 400, reps = 2, seed = 1, args = list(cmi = list(lag = 1), pid = list(lag = 1)))
bv
plot(bv)
```

## Reading the comparisons

* **Stochastic, linear**: Granger-type tests are the most powerful and
  the cheapest; the information-theoretic tests agree but need more
  data.
* **Deterministic**: the embedding-based methods (`dc`, `ccdh`, `cd`,
  `hirata`, `ccm`) see the structure the regression misses; `dc` and
  `ccdh` can name a hidden common cause, `ccm` tends to call strong
  coupling bidirectional.
* **Hidden common drivers**: `cmi_lag` (stochastic), `dc`, `ccdh`,
  `hirata` (deterministic) and the Table-2 reading of `df` are the
  methods that can return `common_cause`; the others can only report the
  absence of a directed link.
* Run `benchmark_methods()` with the simulator closest to your data
  before trusting one method on it; `compare_methods()` then shows where
  the chosen methods agree on the real series.
